subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Mood-Congruent Judgment
description: A short lesson to help you apply Mood-Congruent Judgment.

hook.text: People found a coin on a copy machine. Minutes later, they rated their entire life as more satisfying.

buildup.text: Schwarz showed that incidental mood colors unrelated judgments. A sunny day boosts life satisfaction scores.

discovery.text: Mood-congruent judgment: your current emotional state biases all assessments, not just the related ones.

twist.text: But when people are told it's the weather affecting them, the bias vanishes. Awareness breaks the spell.

climax.text: Before a big decision, ask: is my mood affecting my judgment? Naming the feeling reduces its power.

punchline.text: Check the weather before you judge your life.

quiz.question: What breaks mood-congruent judgment?
options: Making the person aware the mood may be influencing them

details.summary: Mood-congruent judgment means that current mood colors all evaluations and predictions. Happy people judge risks as lower, rate products higher, and predict better outcomes. Sad people see more risk, rate things lower, and expect worse outcomes across unrelated domains.
details.whyItMatters: Mood silently biases evaluations that people believe are objective. A manager in a good mood rates performance reviews higher. An investor feeling anxious perceives more risk.
takeaways: Positive moods lead to more optimistic judgments across all domains
Negative moods create pessimistic evaluations that feel like objective analysis
Important evaluations should be made in neutral mood states when possible

faq.question: How does mood-congruent judgment affect workplace decisions?
faq.answer: Managers in good moods rate employee performance higher, approve risky projects more readily, and are more optimistic about forecasts. The same managers in bad moods produce lower ratings, reject projects, and see more downside. The work has not changed, only the mood.

faq.question: Can awareness of mood-congruent judgment reduce its effect?
faq.answer: Partially. Recognizing that your current mood may be coloring your judgment helps. Delaying important evaluations when in extreme emotional states is more effective. Using structured evaluation criteria reduces the influence of mood on systematic assessments.
